title: Digital Arithmetic: Operations & Circuits
note_on_figures: PDF page-image rendering (pdftoppm/poppler) was unavailable in this environment, so figures could not be visually re-rendered. figure_note fields are reconstructed from the slide's own descriptive captions rather than a pixel-level transcription; treat them as best-effort summaries, not verified transcriptions.

chunks.summary: Binary numbers add and subtract using the same positional-carry/borrow logic as decimal, except the carry threshold is 1 (sum of 1+1) instead of 9; addition is the fundamental operation digital hardware uses to also implement subtraction, multiplication, and division.
chunks.text:
Binary addition follows the same principle as decimal addition: when a column's digits sum to more than the base allows for a single digit, a carry is generated into the next column. In decimal, a carry occurs when a column sums past 9; in binary, a carry occurs whenever a column sums past 1 (i.e. 1+1=10 in binary, producing a sum digit of 0 and a carry of 1). Addition is considered the basic arithmetic operation in digital systems because hardware typically implements subtraction, multiplication, and division all in terms of repeated or modified addition (e.g. subtraction via 2's-complement addition, multiplication via shift-and-add, division via shift-and-subtract), rather than building separate native circuits for each operation.

Binary subtraction works just like decimal subtraction, borrowing from the next higher column when needed. There are four possible cases when subtracting one bit from another bit in any single column of a binary subtraction, accounting for a possible borrow-in from the previous (lower) column and a possible borrow-out to the next (higher) column: 0-0=0 (no borrow), 1-0=1 (no borrow), 1-1=0 (no borrow), and 0-1=1 with a borrow generated from the next column (since 0-1 requires borrowing, giving 10(2)-1=1 with borrow-out=1).
chunks.figure_note: Page 5 tabulates the four possible bit-subtraction cases (with borrow-in/borrow-out) for any single column of a binary subtraction. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the four cases above are standard binary-subtraction theory and match the slide caption.

chunks.topic: Representing Signed Binary Numbers (Sign Bit, 1's/2's Complement)
chunks.summary: Because pure binary only shows magnitude, an extra sign bit (0=positive, 1=negative) is added to represent signed numbers; the 2's-complement system is the most widely used signed representation, obtained by inverting all bits (1's complement) and then adding 1.
chunks.text:
A plain binary number only conveys magnitude, so an extra SIGN BIT is prepended to represent the number's sign: a sign bit of 0 indicates a positive number, and a sign bit of 1 indicates a negative number. The most widely used scheme for representing signed numbers in digital systems is the 2's-complement system (as opposed to sign-magnitude or 1's-complement, which have drawbacks such as dual representations of zero).

To convert a binary number into its 2's-complement (negated) form: first form the 1's complement by inverting (complementing) every bit — changing each 0 to 1 and each 1 to 0. Then form the 2's complement by adding 1 to that 1's-complement result. Negating a number (flipping its sign, e.g. converting +5 to -5 or vice versa) is done precisely by taking the 2's complement of its binary representation — applying the same procedure again (complement, then add 1) converts a 2's-complement negative number back to its positive form, confirming the operation is its own inverse.

chunks.topic: Addition and Subtraction in the 2's-Complement System, and Overflow
chunks.summary: In 2's complement, addition is performed as ordinary binary addition including the sign bit, discarding any carry out of the sign bit; subtraction is done by negating the subtrahend and adding. Overflow (an incorrect result) can only occur when adding two numbers of the SAME sign, and is detected when the result's magnitude exceeds what the available magnitude bits can represent.
chunks.text:
Addition in the 2's-complement system is performed by simply carrying out normal binary addition across ALL the bits, including the sign bit — the sign bit is added right along with the magnitude bits, with no special-case handling required. If this addition produces a carry OUT of the sign-bit position, that carry is simply discarded/ignored (it does not indicate an error by itself). If the resulting sign bit of the sum is 0, the result is positive and is already in ordinary (pure) binary form; if the resulting sign bit is 1, the result is negative and is expressed in 2's-complement form (so it would need to be re-complemented to read off its magnitude in ordinary binary, if desired).

Subtraction in the 2's-complement system is performed as addition: rather than building a separate subtractor circuit, the subtrahend (the number being subtracted) is first negated (2's-complemented), and this negated value is then ADDED to the minuend using the same addition procedure above; the resulting sum represents the difference. This is precisely why 2's complement is so useful in hardware — one adder circuit, plus a way to conditionally complement one operand, implements both addition and subtraction.

Overflow occurs when the true mathematical result of an addition cannot be represented correctly within the available number of magnitude bits (plus sign bit) — this can ONLY happen when adding two numbers of the SAME sign (two positives or two negatives); adding numbers of opposite sign can never overflow, because the true result's magnitude is always smaller than (or equal to) the larger operand's magnitude. When overflow occurs, the addition produces an incorrect (garbage) result and must be flagged. A helpful way to visualize this is a 'number circle': represent the augend as a starting position, and add the addend by advancing clockwise around the circle by that many spaces (subtraction correspondingly moves counterclockwise). For a signed 4-bit representation, any subtraction (or by extension, any same-sign addition) between numbers that produces a mathematically true result greater than +7 or less than -8 is, by definition, an overflow, since 4-bit signed values can only represent the range -8 to +7.
chunks.figure_note: Page 11 shows a circular ('number circle') diagram for 4-bit signed numbers (-8 to +7 arranged around a circle), illustrating clockwise movement for addition and counterclockwise movement for subtraction, and marking which resulting positions represent an overflow. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the overflow rule ('only for same-sign operands, when the true result exceeds the representable range') is standard 2's-complement arithmetic and independently verifiable.

chunks.summary: Binary multiplication mirrors decimal long multiplication: each multiplier bit multiplies the entire multiplicand (trivial since bits are 0 or 1), each partial product is shifted one position left as you move from the multiplier's LSB toward its MSB, and all partial products are summed to get the final result.
chunks.text: Binary multiplication is performed the same way as decimal (long-hand) multiplication: each bit of the multiplier, in turn, multiplies the entire multiplicand, producing one partial product per multiplier bit (in binary this step is trivial — multiplying by a 0 bit gives an all-zero partial product, multiplying by a 1 bit gives a copy of the multiplicand unchanged). As you proceed from the multiplier's least-significant bit (LSB) toward its most-significant bit (MSB), each successive partial product is shifted one additional bit position to the left (exactly as decimal long multiplication shifts each partial product left one digit position). Finally, all of the (shifted) partial products are added together (using ordinary binary addition) to produce the final product.

chunks.summary: Binary division mirrors decimal long division but is simpler since each quotient digit can only be 0 or 1; the repeated subtraction step is carried out using 2's-complement subtraction, and the quotient's sign follows the usual same-sign-positive/different-sign-negative rule.
chunks.text: Binary division is performed similarly to decimal long division, but is actually simpler in binary because at each step the quotient digit being determined can only be 0 or 1 (rather than 0 through 9), which removes the 'guess the digit' difficulty of decimal long division. The repeated subtract step inherent to long division is carried out using 2's-complement subtraction (i.e., negate the divisor and add, per Section 6-4) rather than a dedicated subtractor. Sign handling follows the ordinary rule of signed division: if the dividend and divisor have the SAME sign, the quotient (answer) is positive; if they have DIFFERENT signs, the quotient is negative.

chunks.summary: Adding two BCD (Binary-Coded Decimal) digits proceeds as ordinary 4-bit binary addition when the sum is 9 or less; when the sum of a decimal-digit pair exceeds 9, a correction of adding binary 6 (0110) must be applied, which always produces a carry into the next BCD digit.
chunks.text: In BCD (Binary-Coded Decimal) addition, each decimal digit is represented by its own 4-bit binary code (0000 through 1001 for digits 0-9), and digit-pairs are added independently, digit position by digit position. When the raw binary sum of a given decimal-digit pair (plus any carry-in) is 9 or less, the operation is identical to ordinary binary addition and the 4-bit result is already valid BCD. However, when the raw binary sum of a decimal-digit pair exceeds 9 (i.e., the 4-bit binary result falls into the 1010-1111 range, which has no valid BCD meaning, or a carry-out of the 4-bit group already occurred), a correction is required: add binary 6 (0110) to that digit's result. This correction of adding 6 will ALWAYS produce a carry out of that 4-bit group into the next-higher BCD digit position, which is exactly the correct decimal carry behavior (mirroring how decimal addition carries once a column reaches 10).

chunks.summary: Hex addition sums digit pairs in decimal, expressing sums of 15 or less directly in hex and, for sums greater than 15, subtracting 16 and carrying 1; hex subtraction uses the same borrow method as binary/decimal; a hex number's sign (in signed representations) is read from its most-significant hex digit (8-F = negative, 0-7 = positive).
chunks.text:
Hexadecimal addition: add each pair of hex digits by first converting mentally to their decimal values, summing in decimal, then converting back — if the decimal sum is 15 or less, it is expressed directly as a single hex digit (0-F); if the decimal sum exceeds 15, subtract 16 from it (to get the digit that is written down) and carry a 1 into the next higher hex position (exactly analogous to carrying when a decimal column exceeds 9, or a binary column exceeds 1).

Hexadecimal subtraction uses the same borrowing method used for binary and decimal subtraction, adapted to base 16. For signed hexadecimal numbers, the sign is read from the Most Significant hex Digit (MSD): if the MSD is 8 or greater (8 through F), the number is negative; if the MSD is 7 or less (0 through 7), the number is positive — this directly mirrors the binary sign-bit convention, since a hex digit of 8 or above always has its own most-significant BIT equal to 1.

chunks.topic: Arithmetic Circuits and the ALU Concept
chunks.summary: An arithmetic/logic unit (ALU) accepts operand data from memory and an accumulator register, performs arithmetic/logic operations as directed by a control unit, and writes the result back to the accumulator — illustrated by a step-by-step trace of adding a memory value to an accumulator value.
chunks.text: An Arithmetic/Logic Unit (ALU) accepts data stored in memory and performs arithmetic and logic operations on it as instructed by a control unit, which orchestrates the sequence of register transfers and operations needed to carry out a given instruction (e.g. 'add this memory value to the accumulator'). A representative operation sequence for adding a memory value into an accumulator register proceeds in steps: (1) the control unit is instructed to add a specific number, located at a given memory address, into the number already held in the accumulator register; (2) that number is transferred from memory into an intermediate holding register (the B register); (3) the ALU's logic circuit adds the contents of the B register and the accumulator register together, and the resulting sum is sent to (and stored in) the accumulator; (4) the new (updated) number now resides in the accumulator, ready either for further operations or for being transferred out to memory for storage.
chunks.figure_note: Pages 17-20 show a sequence of block diagrams tracing the add-to-accumulator operation: memory -> B register -> ALU adder (with accumulator) -> updated accumulator -> optional write-back to memory. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.summary: A parallel adder adds two multi-bit binary numbers at once by chaining one full adder per bit position; a five-bit parallel adder, for example, is built from five cascaded full-adder stages.
chunks.text: Computers and calculators need to add two multi-bit binary numbers together in a single operation rather than one bit at a time. A parallel adder accomplishes this by using one Full Adder (FA) circuit per bit position, with the carry-out of each stage wired into the carry-in of the next-higher-order stage — this lets all bit positions be summed together with carries rippling automatically through the chain. A representative example is a five-bit parallel adder built from five cascaded full-adder stages, each handling one bit of the two 5-bit operands plus the incoming carry from the stage below it.
chunks.figure_note: Page 22 shows a block diagram of a 5-bit parallel adder built from five full-adder (FA) blocks, with carry lines connecting each stage's carry-out to the next stage's carry-in. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.summary: A full adder is designed like any combinational circuit: build a truth table with 3 inputs (two operand bits A, B, and carry-in Cin) and 2 outputs (Sum and carry-out Cout), then derive/simplify SOP expressions (algebraically or via K-map). The standard results are Sum = A XOR B XOR Cin and Cout = AB + Cin(A XOR B) [equivalently AB + BCin + ACin].
chunks.text:
A full adder is designed using the standard combinational-design procedure from Chapter 4: construct a truth table with 3 inputs — the two bits being added (A and B) and a carry-in (Cin) from the previous (lower-order) bit position — and 2 outputs — the Sum bit and a carry-out (Cout) to the next (higher-order) bit position. The 8-row truth table for a full adder is: A=0,B=0,Cin=0 -> Sum=0,Cout=0; A=0,B=0,Cin=1 -> Sum=1,Cout=0; A=0,B=1,Cin=0 -> Sum=1,Cout=0; A=0,B=1,Cin=1 -> Sum=0,Cout=1; A=1,B=0,Cin=0 -> Sum=1,Cout=0; A=1,B=0,Cin=1 -> Sum=0,Cout=1; A=1,B=1,Cin=0 -> Sum=0,Cout=1; A=1,B=1,Cin=1 -> Sum=1,Cout=1.

Using algebraic methods or a K-map to simplify the resulting SOP expressions gives the standard, minimal full-adder equations: Sum = A XOR B XOR Cin (Sum is 1 whenever an odd number of the three inputs are 1), and Cout = AB + ACin + BCin (Cout is 1 whenever at least two of the three inputs are 1) — equivalently written Cout = AB + Cin(A XOR B). The resulting logic circuit is typically implemented as two cascaded XOR gates (for Sum) plus an AND/OR network (for Cout), or equivalently as two half-adders plus an OR gate. This full-adder building block is what gets replicated to build the parallel (multi-bit) adder of Section 6-10.
chunks.figure_note: Page 24 shows the resulting full-adder gate-level circuit (XOR/AND/OR network implementing Sum and Cout). Truth table and equations above were independently re-derived and verified by enumeration (all 8 rows), matching standard full-adder theory; not visually re-verified pixel-by-pixel since PDF rendering is unavailable here.

chunks.topic: Complete Parallel Adder With Storage Registers
chunks.summary: A practical 4-bit parallel adder includes storage registers (A and B) around the adder logic; a worked timing trace shows adding 1001 and 0101 via a sequence of clear, load-B, add-to-A, load-B-again, add-to-A-again steps, ending with the sum in the accumulator (A register).
chunks.text:
A complete, practical parallel adder circuit combines a chain of full adders with storage registers: a 4-bit example includes an A register (the accumulator, which also receives the sum output) and a B register (holding the second operand), with the full-adder chain positioned between them.

Worked timing example, adding binary 1001 + 0101 using this circuit: at time t1, a CLR (clear) pulse resets the A register to 0000. At t2, the first operand, 1001, is transferred from memory into the B register. At t3, the adder computes the sum of the current A register (0000) and B register (1001) — namely 1001 — and this sum is transferred (loaded) into the A register, so [A] becomes 1001. At t4, the second operand, 0101, is transferred from memory into the B register (overwriting the first operand there). At t5, the adder's sum outputs (now A=1001 plus B=0101 = 1110) are transferred into the A register. After this sequence, the sum of the two original numbers (1001+0101=1110) is present in the accumulator (A register).

Notation used for describing register contents and transfers: square brackets denote 'the contents of' a register, e.g. [A]=1011 means register A currently holds the 4-bit value 1011 (i.e., A3=1, A2=0, A1=1, A0=1). An arrow denotes a transfer operation, e.g. [B] -> [A] reads as 'the contents of register B have been transferred to register A.'
chunks.figure_note: Page 25 shows the block diagram of the 4-bit parallel adder including the A (accumulator) and B storage registers surrounding the full-adder chain. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the t1-t5 timing trace above is transcribed and re-checked arithmetically (1001+0101=1110) against the slide text.

chunks.summary: A parallel adder's maximum speed is limited by carry propagation (carry ripple): each stage's sum can't be considered final until its carry-in has settled, so the total delay grows with the number of bits; look-ahead carry logic is the common technique used in high-speed adders to reduce this delay.
chunks.text: The speed of a ripple-carry parallel adder is fundamentally limited by carry propagation, also called carry ripple: the final, correct carry-out of the most-significant stage cannot be guaranteed until the carry has had time to 'ripple' sequentially through every lower-order full-adder stage below it (since each stage's carry-out depends on its own carry-in, which depends on the stage before it, and so on down the chain). Adding more bits to the adder therefore introduces proportionally more worst-case propagation delay before the final sum/carry is valid, which becomes a real performance bottleneck for wide (e.g. 32-bit, 64-bit) adders. The standard technique to address this in high-speed adder designs is look-ahead carry (carry-lookahead) logic, which computes each stage's carry directly from the original input bits (using additional combinational logic) rather than waiting for it to ripple through every intermediate stage, substantially reducing the worst-case delay at the cost of extra gate complexity.

chunks.topic: Integrated Circuit Parallel Adders (4-bit adder chips, cascading)
chunks.summary: The most common commercial parallel adder is a 4-bit IC containing 4 interconnected full adders plus internal look-ahead-carry logic; example parts include the 7483A, 74LS83A, 74LS283, and 74HC283, each with A/B 4-bit inputs, a carry-in (C0), a carry-out (C4), and a 4-bit sum output; these chips can be cascaded (e.g. two chips) to add wider numbers such as two 8-bit values.
chunks.text:
The most common commercially available parallel adder IC is a 4-bit device, internally consisting of 4 interconnected full-adder stages plus built-in look-ahead-carry circuitry to keep the 4-bit addition fast. Standard 4-bit parallel-adder chip part numbers mentioned include the 7483A, 74LS83A, 74LS283, and 74HC283 (functionally similar/interchangeable across TTL/CMOS families with generally compatible pinouts within a family). Pin conventions: the A input lines and B input lines each represent one 4-bit operand to be added; C0 is the carry-in to the least-significant bit position; C4 is the carry-out from the most-significant bit position; and a 4-bit Sum output provides the result.

Multiple 4-bit adder chips can be cascaded together (chaining each chip's C4 carry-out into the next chip's C0 carry-in) to build adders for wider operands than a single chip supports — for example, two 4-bit adder chips cascaded together can add two 8-bit numbers, and this cascading pattern extends to any multiple of 4 bits by adding more chips in the chain.
chunks.figure_note: Page 30 shows the pinout/block symbol of a 4-bit adder IC with A[3:0], B[3:0], C0, C4, and Sum[3:0] labeled. Page 31 shows two such chips cascaded (C4 of the low chip into C0 of the high chip) to add two 8-bit numbers. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.summary: A single parallel-adder circuit can perform both addition and subtraction of 2's-complement numbers by selectively 2's-complementing the B operand; two control lines, ADD and SUB, select the operation — ADD performs A+B normally, SUB computes A minus B by complementing B before adding.
chunks.text:
Adding a negative (2's-complement) number to a positive number with a standard adder is done simply by first converting the negative number into its 2's-complement bit pattern and then performing ordinary addition — no special adder hardware is needed for signed addition beyond the 2's-complement encoding itself. An adder can ALSO be used to perform SUBTRACTION, by adding extra logic that conditionally forms the 2's complement of one operand (the subtrahend, B) before it enters the adder, so that A + (2's-complement of B) computes A - B using the very same adder hardware.

This leads to a combined adder/subtractor circuit controlled by two control signals, ADD and SUB: when ADD is HIGH, the circuit performs straightforward addition of the numbers stored in the A and B registers (A+B); when SUB is HIGH, the circuit instead subtracts the B-register number from the A-register number (A-B), by internally complementing B (typically via XOR gates that pass B unchanged when ADD is active but invert every B bit when SUB is active, combined with feeding the SUB signal into the adder's initial carry-in to complete the 2's-complement '+1') before it enters the same adder used for the ADD case. This is the parallel adder/subtractor circuit using the 2's-complement system depicted on the corresponding slide.
chunks.figure_note: Page 35 shows the complete parallel adder/subtractor schematic: A and B registers feeding a full-adder chain, with XOR gates conditionally inverting the B bits and the SUB signal feeding the adder's carry-in, controlled by the ADD/SUB select lines. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the XOR-based complementing mechanism described is standard textbook 2's-complement adder/subtractor design.

chunks.summary: Commercial ALU ICs perform a selectable set of arithmetic and logic functions on their input data, chosen via a binary code applied to dedicated function-select input pins; the 74LS382 (TTL) / 74HC382 (CMOS) is cited as a typical example offering 8 selectable functions.
chunks.text: A commercial Arithmetic/Logic Unit (ALU) IC can perform several different arithmetic operations (such as add, subtract, increment) and logic operations (such as AND, OR, XOR) on its input operands, with the SPECIFIC operation performed at any given time selected by a binary code applied to the device's dedicated function-select input pins — the same physical hardware can be reconfigured on the fly to perform whichever operation the select code specifies. A representative example cited is the 74LS382 (TTL family) and its CMOS counterpart the 74HC382, which offers 8 selectable functions controlled by a 3-bit function-select code.
chunks.figure_note: Page 37 shows the 74LS382/74HC382 pinout and its function table (listing which 3-bit select code corresponds to which of the 8 arithmetic/logic operations). Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here.

chunks.summary: A three-mode fault-diagnosis exercise on the 2's-complement adder/subtractor circuit: in Mode 1 (ADD=0,SUB=0, i.e. neither control active) the sum outputs are consistently one more than the A register value; in Mode 2 (ADD=1,SUB=0) the sum is consistently one more than expected; in Mode 3 (ADD=0,SUB=1) the outputs correctly equal [A]-[B] — pointing toward a stuck carry-in fault.
chunks.text:
This is a worked troubleshooting exercise on the parallel adder/subtractor circuit from Section 6-15, observed across its three control-line modes: Mode 1 (ADD=0, SUB=0 — an inactive/undefined control combination): the sum outputs are observed to always equal the number in the A register PLUS ONE, rather than the expected behavior for that mode. Mode 2 (ADD=1, SUB=0 — normal addition mode): the sum is observed to always be exactly one more than it should be (i.e., every A+B result reads one too high). Mode 3 (ADD=0, SUB=1 — subtraction mode): the outputs correctly equal [A]-[B] as expected, with no fault apparent in this mode. 

The diagnostic pattern across these three modes — correct in SUB mode but consistently '+1' too high in the two modes where SUB is inactive — points toward a fault where the adder's carry-in line is stuck HIGH (since the SUB control line, when active, is supposed to drive carry-in HIGH deliberately as part of forming the 2's complement, and this happens to coincide with correct behavior in Mode 3 but manifests as a spurious '+1' error whenever SUB should be LOW/inactive). This exercise reinforces the general troubleshooting approach: exercise a faulty circuit systematically across ALL of its defined control-input modes and look for a consistent pattern in how the observed behavior deviates from the expected behavior, which usually points directly at the specific stuck-at or shorted node responsible.
chunks.figure_note: The three pages show the same adder/subtractor circuit exercised under the three ADD/SUB mode combinations described. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the stuck-carry-in diagnosis above is my own inference from the pattern of symptoms described in the slide text (correct only when SUB=1), not explicitly stated as the answer on the slide — flagged here as inferred rather than verbatim.

chunks.topic: Using TTL Library Functions with Altera, and Logical Operations on Bit Arrays in HDL
chunks.summary: Altera's development tools offer pre-defined logic-function macrofunctions (e.g. ALUs can be instantiated graphically) so designers can reuse standard building blocks; separately, HDLs represent multi-bit signals as bit arrays and provide Boolean operators (AND/OR/XOR/etc.) that act across an entire array at once, with slightly different array syntax between AHDL and VHDL.
chunks.text:
Altera's development environment provides pre-defined logic circuits packaged as macrofunctions, letting designers instantiate common building blocks (such as an ALU) directly rather than re-implementing them from primitive gates every time. Such devices may be defined either graphically (via schematic-style symbol instantiation) or textually using macrofunction calls in HDL code; although the graphic approach can feel more intuitive at first, defining a device via text/macrofunctions is often actually easier and more maintainable in practice, especially for parameterized or repeated instantiation.

Separately, effective HDL design requires understanding two related techniques: (1) specifying groups of bits as arrays (bit vectors) and (2) applying logical/Boolean operations across those arrays as a unit. HDLs represent multi-bit signals using an array-of-bits notation similar to register notation. For example, a 4-bit signal named d can be declared in AHDL as `VARIABLE d[3..0] : NODE;` and in VHDL as `SIGNAL d : BIT_VECTOR (3 DOWNTO 1);` (note VHDL's DOWNTO range syntax explicitly states the bit-index bounds, here shown spanning bits 3 down to 1 in the slide's example). Once declared this way, standard Boolean operators (AND, OR, XOR, NOT, etc.) can typically be applied to the entire bit-array signal in a single expression, letting the HDL compiler implement the equivalent per-bit gate array automatically instead of the designer writing one gate instantiation per individual bit.
chunks.figure_note: Page 41 shows a graphical ALU macrofunction block being instantiated in Altera's schematic-entry tool. Not visually re-verified since PDF rendering unavailable here; the AHDL/VHDL bit-array declaration syntax above is transcribed directly from the slide text.

chunks.topic: HDL Adders (8-bit Parallel Adder in AHDL and VHDL)
chunks.summary: An 8-bit parallel adder is described in HDL by declaring 8-bit input arrays A[8..1] and B[8..1] and computing their sum into a 9-bit output array (extra bit for the final carry-out), shown in both AHDL and VHDL syntax.
chunks.text: This section presents an 8-bit parallel adder circuit written directly in HDL, in both AHDL and VHDL variants, illustrating how the bit-array techniques from Section 6-19 are applied to a concrete, useful circuit. The design takes two 8-bit input values, named A[8..1] and B[8..1] (using the slide's 1-indexed bit-numbering convention), and produces a 9-BIT sum output — the extra (ninth) bit is needed to correctly represent the final carry-out that can result from adding two 8-bit numbers (the maximum possible sum of two 8-bit unsigned values needs 9 bits to represent without overflow/wraparound). The AHDL version and the VHDL version both express this same '9-bit-out = 8-bit-A + 8-bit-B' relationship, just using each language's own array-declaration and addition-operator syntax (VHDL typically uses the '+' operator directly on BIT_VECTOR/std_logic_vector signals once appropriate types/libraries are used; AHDL uses its own array and arithmetic-expression syntax).
chunks.figure_note: Pages 43 and 44 show the actual AHDL and VHDL source-code listings respectively for the 8-bit adder. The literal code text could not be transcribed because PDF page-image rendering is unavailable in this environment; the functional description above (8-bit A + 8-bit B -> 9-bit sum) is accurately derived from the slide captions, but the exact code syntax on these 2 pages should be re-transcribed once a PDF renderer is available before treating it as a verified code sample.

chunks.topic: Parameterizing the Bit Capacity of a Circuit (Constants, add_sub control, LPMs)
chunks.summary: HDL constants let a circuit's bit-width be defined once as a named symbol and reused throughout the code, so the design can be resized by changing a single line; a worked adder/subtractor example adds a single add_sub control bit (0=add, 1=subtract) with overflow checking, declared via CONSTANT in AHDL and VHDL; Altera's Library of Parameterized Modules (LPMs) provides ready-made generic building blocks.
chunks.text:
A CONSTANT in HDL is a fixed value represented by a symbolic name, typically defined once near the top of the source file (e.g. defining a name for the total number of bits in a design) and then referenced throughout the rest of the code wherever that value is needed. The benefit is maintainability: to resize or otherwise modify the circuit later, only that single constant-definition line needs to be edited, rather than hunting down and changing every literal occurrence of the bit-width value throughout the code.

Worked example: adding a parameterized 'constant feature' to the HDL code for an adder/subtractor circuit (extending the circuit from Section 6-15/6-20), controlled by a single input bit named add_sub: when add_sub = 0, the circuit adds the two operands; when add_sub = 1, it subtracts b from a. The design also includes logic to check for overflow in the case of signed-number operations, flagging when the result cannot be correctly represented in the available bit width. 

In AHDL, this parameterization is expressed with the keyword CONSTANT followed by the symbolic name and the value being assigned to it. In VHDL, the equivalent is also introduced with the keyword CONSTANT, but additionally requires specifying the constant's TYPE along with its symbolic name and assigned value (VHDL being more strongly typed than AHDL). VHDL additionally offers a GENERATE statement, which can concisely replicate several identical components (such as the individual full-adder stages that make up a parallel adder) that are meant to be cascaded together, without the designer having to write out each instance by hand.

Beyond hand-written parameterized HDL, Altera also offers a Library of Parameterized Modules (LPMs) — pre-built, generic solutions for common logic-circuit building blocks (adders, counters, multiplexers, memories, etc.) used throughout digital system design, where the designer supplies parameters (such as bit width) to an existing, verified module rather than writing the underlying HDL from scratch.
